content: Suma root, also known as Brazilian ginseng, is derived from the root of a sprawling ground vine native to South America. Its scientific names include Pfaffia paniculata, Hebanthe paniculata, Gomphrena paniculata, and several others. Traditionally, it has been used as a medicinal herb and tonic. It is often referred to as para todo, meaning for all, due to its adaptogenic properties, which help regulate and enhance bodily systems, improve stress resistance, and promote overall health. Suma has been employed to address a wide range of health conditions with notable effectiveness, justifying its nickname. Pharmacology and Mechanism of Action Suma is believed to support hormonal balance, reduce inflammation, inhibit the growth of cancer and leukemia cells, enhance immune function, and increase libido. It also provides various normalizing and rejuvenating effects. One potential explanation for its broad range of benefits is its ability to improve oxygenation and energy efficiency at the cellular level. The root contains several bioactive compounds, including germanium, beta-ecdysterone, allantoin, and a unique group of saponins known as pfaffosides. Historical Use and Research The use of Iresine celosia, a related species, dates back approximately 2,000 years to the Maya-Quiché civilization. This plant is mentioned in the 1552 manuscript Libellus de Medicinalibus Indorum Herbis, which documents pre-Columbian medicinal practices. In modern times, during the 1960s to 1980s, Efraín Contreras, a renowned naturopath, identified the anti-tumoral properties of Iresine celosia, a plant native to Central America. He received approval to administer Iresine celosia in both liquid and dry extract forms to patients in Nicaraguan hospitals, including Hospital El Retiro and Hospital Bertha Calderón. In 1983, the Scientific Commission of the Ministry of Health of Nicaragua evaluated the effects of Iresine celosia, referred to as Codin VII. The herbal extract was administered to patients with digestive system tumors, both preand post-surgery. The results showed significant tumor size reduction, including cases of stomach carcinomas and regional lymph node involvement. In surgeries involving mammary gland carcinomas and metastases, local metastases disappeared within 12 to 15 days of treatment, and distant metastases were also reduced. Across all cases, patients experienced marked improvements in general health, with symptoms such as hemorrhages, vaginal discharges, and pain resolving. Importantly, no toxicity or adverse effects were observed. During the 1990s, Iresine celosia was also used to treat prostate issues and sexual impotence, yielding promising outcomes. Research conducted by Pierre Crabbé, P.R. Leeming, and Carl Djerassi at Wayne State University contributed to understanding the structure of the isoflavone Tlatlancuayin, a compound found in the plant. Iresine celosia was introduced to Europe approximately 15 years ago. In 1994, Edda Contreras, the daughter of Efraín Contreras, collaborated with the European Institute of Tropical Phytotherapy. Between 1994 and 1998, the plant was presented at various forums in France, including Cannes, Sophia Antipolis, Biarritz, Lyon, and Paris. Historically, Iresine celosia has been used to treat tumors in the prostate, mammary glands, ovaries, brain, and intestines. It has also been employed to enhance libido, address psychiatric conditions, and support individuals with immune system deficiencies. Active Compounds and Mechanism of Action Iresine celosia contains 2.50% natural glucid steroids. Clinical studies conducted in Nicaragua demonstrated that the plant alters the permeability of pathological cells and modifies the bioelectric potential of cancerous cell membranes. These effects may underlie its therapeutic benefits in treating cancer and other conditions.
